title: Flip-Flop
body:
A one-bit storage element that samples its input on a **clock edge** rather than a clock
level. That single difference from the [[D-Latch]] is what makes large
[[Synchronous]] circuits buildable.

| | Triggered by | Behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| [[D-Latch]] | **Level** | Transparent: while enable is high, $Q$ follows $D$ |
| **Flip-flop** | **Edge** | $Q$ takes the value $D$ had at the clock edge, then holds until the next one |

The usual construction is two D-latches in series with opposite enable polarity
(master-slave): the master is transparent while the clock is low, the slave while it is
high, so a value can only make it all the way through by crossing an edge.

**Why edges matter.** In an edge-triggered design every element updates at the same
instant and then holds still. The [[Combinational Logic]] between flip-flops has the whole
clock period to settle, and no signal can race through two stages in one cycle. That gives
you the standard timing rule: the clock period must exceed the longest combinational path
plus setup time, which is where a chip's maximum clock speed comes from.

Feed $D$ from the input and you get a D flip-flop; other flavours (JK, T) differ only in
what function of the inputs and current state drives $D$. Chain several so each one's $Q$
feeds the next one's $D$ and you get a [[Shift Register]]. Add
[[Combinational Logic]] computing the next state from the current one and you have a
[[Finite State Machine]], which is what a [[CPU]]'s control unit is.

Violate the setup or hold window and the flip-flop can go [[metastability|metastable]].
